metrics.label: RSRP
metrics.whatItMeasures: Reference Signal Received Power — the strength of the cellular signal from the tower to your phone.
metrics.currentValueContext: Measured in dBm (decibel-milliwatts). Higher (less negative) = stronger signal.
metrics.healthyRange: -80 dBm to -100 dBm is good. Below -120 dBm is very weak.
metrics.commonCauses: Thick walls, basement, distance from tower, building materials, network congestion.

metrics.label: RSRQ
metrics.whatItMeasures: Reference Signal Received Quality — the quality of the received signal, factoring in interference and noise.
metrics.currentValueContext: Measured in dB. Higher (less negative) = better quality.
metrics.healthyRange: -5 dB to -10 dB is good. Below -15 dB indicates significant interference.
metrics.commonCauses: Network congestion, interference from other cell towers, physical obstructions causing signal reflections.

metrics.label: SINR
metrics.whatItMeasures: Signal to Interference plus Noise Ratio — how clean your signal is versus background noise and interference.
metrics.currentValueContext: Measured in dB. Higher = cleaner signal. This is the best indicator of actual data performance.
metrics.healthyRange: 13 dB+ is excellent. 5-13 dB is good. Below 5 dB means poor conditions.
metrics.commonCauses: Edge of cell coverage, interference from other towers, building materials, many users on the same tower.

metrics.label: Active Band
metrics.whatItMeasures: The specific frequency band your phone is currently connected to for cellular service.
metrics.currentValueContext: Bands are numbered — n71 is low-band 5G (better range), n78 is mid-band 5G (faster speeds), B41 is mid-band 4G LTE.
metrics.healthyRange: Any connected band is normal. Some bands are faster but shorter range.
metrics.commonCauses: Your carrier determines which bands are available in your area. Phone switches bands automatically based on signal and congestion.

metrics.label: IMS Registration
metrics.whatItMeasures: IP Multimedia Subsystem registration — whether your phone can use VoLTE (voice over 4G/5G) and WiFi Calling.
metrics.currentValueContext: When registered, calls use data networks. When not registered, calls fall back to older 2G/3G networks.
metrics.healthyRange: Registered = good. Not registered = calls may drop or fail.
metrics.commonCauses: Carrier provisioning issue, incorrect APN settings, roaming on a network that doesn't support your IMS profile, software bug.

metrics.label: Network Type
metrics.whatItMeasures: The generation and type of cellular network your phone is currently using for data.
metrics.currentValueContext: NR = 5G, LTE = 4G, HSPA = 3G, EDGE/GPRS = 2G. Faster generations deliver better speeds.
metrics.healthyRange: NR or LTE is normal for modern smartphones.
metrics.commonCauses: Network coverage area, carrier settings, phone capabilities, network congestion, data saver mode.

metrics.label: Roaming
metrics.whatItMeasures: Whether your phone is connected to a network other than your primary carrier's home network.
metrics.currentValueContext: On = you're using another carrier's network. May incur extra charges depending on your plan.
metrics.healthyRange: Off is normal when not travelling. On is expected when abroad or in areas without your carrier's coverage.
metrics.commonCauses: International travel, remote area with no home carrier coverage, network outage on your carrier.

metrics.label: Cell ID (eCID)
metrics.whatItMeasures: A unique identifier for the specific cell tower sector your phone is connected to.
metrics.currentValueContext: This number identifies which physical tower you're connected to. Useful for tracking coverage patterns.
metrics.healthyRange: Any value is normal. Frequent changes mean you're moving or the network is handing you off between towers.
metrics.commonCauses: Walking or driving between cell coverage areas, network load balancing.

metrics.label: Battery Level
metrics.whatItMeasures: The current charge level of your phone's battery as a percentage of its capacity.
metrics.currentValueContext: 0% = empty, 100% = full charge. Below 20% most phones enter low-power mode.
metrics.healthyRange: 20-100% is normal operating range.
metrics.commonCauses: Usage patterns, screen brightness, background processes, cellular signal strength (weak signal drains more), battery age.

metrics.label: Battery Health
metrics.whatItMeasures: The physical condition of your battery as reported by the built-in fuel gauge chip.
metrics.currentValueContext: Good = normal. Overheat = too hot, may limit charging. Dead = needs replacement. Cold = below operating temperature.
metrics.healthyRange: Good is the only normal reading for a healthy battery.
metrics.commonCauses: Battery age (lithium batteries degrade after 2-3 years), physical damage, extreme temperatures, manufacturing defect.

metrics.label: Charge Rate
metrics.whatItMeasures: How fast your battery is currently charging or discharging, in microamps.
metrics.currentValueContext: Positive = charging. Negative = discharging. Zero = not connected to power and not draining.
metrics.healthyRange: Charging: 1,000,000-3,000,000 µA is typical. Discharging: -100,000 to -500,000 µA is normal screen-on drain.
metrics.commonCauses: Charger speed, cable quality, battery temperature (charging slows when hot), background activity.

metrics.label: Power Consumption by App
metrics.whatItMeasures: Estimated power draw attributed to each running app and system process.
metrics.currentValueContext: Higher values mean that app is draining more battery. Based on estimated power profiles, not direct measurement.
metrics.healthyRange: Screen usually consumes 30-50% of total. Background apps should be under 5% each.
metrics.commonCauses: App actively doing work, background sync, location services, poor network causing retries, buggy app keeping CPU awake.

metrics.label: CPU Load
metrics.whatItMeasures: How busy each CPU core is, as a percentage of its maximum capacity.
metrics.currentValueContext: 0.0 = idle. 1.0 = completely busy. Most phones have 8 cores (4 efficiency + 4 performance).
metrics.healthyRange: Idle: under 0.1 per core. Normal usage: 0.2-0.5. Heavy gaming/editing: 0.8-1.0.
metrics.commonCauses: Running apps, background processes, system updates, malware, thermal throttling reducing max speed.

metrics.label: Memory Pressure
metrics.whatItMeasures: How constrained the system is by available RAM. High pressure means apps will be killed to free memory.
metrics.currentValueContext: Normal = plenty of RAM. Moderate = system is starting to reclaim memory. Critical = apps are being killed.
metrics.healthyRange: Normal is best. Brief Moderate is OK. Critical means you should close some apps.
metrics.commonCauses: Too many apps running, memory leak in an app, very large app (game or editor), outdated phone with limited RAM.

metrics.label: Storage Used
metrics.whatItMeasures: How much of your internal storage is occupied by apps, media, system files, and cached data.
metrics.currentValueContext: Shown as used vs total. Also broken down by system vs user data for clarity.
metrics.healthyRange: Under 80% full is comfortable. Above 90% the system may slow down. Above 95% you'll get warnings.
metrics.commonCauses: Photos and videos, large games, cached streaming data, downloaded content, system updates.

metrics.label: SIM Provisioning
metrics.whatItMeasures: Whether your SIM or eSIM is activated and ready for service on your carrier's network.
metrics.currentValueContext: Provisioned = ready to use. Not provisioned = SIM may not be activated with your carrier.
metrics.healthyRange: Provisioned is the only normal state for active service.
metrics.commonCauses: New SIM not yet activated, eSIM download incomplete, carrier provisioning delay, SIM card failure.

metrics.label: eSIM Profiles
metrics.whatItMeasures: The number of eSIM profiles installed on your device. Each profile represents a carrier subscription.
metrics.currentValueContext: One profile per active eSIM line. Multiple profiles can be installed but only two (usually) active at once.
metrics.healthyRange: 1-2 profiles is typical. Power users may have 3-5 for travel.
metrics.commonCauses: Adding travel eSIMs, switching carriers, work/personal dual-SIM setup, left old profiles installed.

metrics.label: IP Address
metrics.whatItMeasures: Your device's current IP address on the network — unique identifier for sending and receiving data.
metrics.currentValueContext: IPv4 shown as four numbers separated by dots. IPv6 shown as hexadecimal. Multiple addresses means multiple network interfaces.
metrics.healthyRange: Any valid IP address is normal. If no IP is shown, you're not connected to any network.
metrics.commonCauses: DHCP assignment from router, carrier-assigned IP for mobile data, VPN assigning a new IP, IP address conflict.

metrics.label: Active Network
metrics.whatItMeasures: Which network interface your phone is currently using for internet traffic.
metrics.currentValueContext: WiFi = connected to a wireless network. Mobile = using cellular data. VPN = all traffic going through VPN tunnel.
metrics.healthyRange: Any is normal. WiFi is usually faster and uses less battery than mobile data.
metrics.commonCauses: WiFi range, mobile data enabled, VPN app active, airplane mode, hotspot/tethering active.

metrics.label: Temperature
metrics.whatItMeasures: The temperature of various components inside your phone — CPU, battery, modem, and others.
metrics.currentValueContext: Multiple zones monitored independently. The hottest zone typically determines whether the phone throttles.
metrics.healthyRange: Under 40°C is cool. 40-55°C is warm. Above 55°C may trigger throttling to protect components.
metrics.commonCauses: Heavy gaming or video, direct sunlight, fast charging, poor case ventilation, faulty battery.

metrics.label: Throttling
metrics.whatItMeasures: Whether the system is intentionally reducing performance to lower temperature and protect components.
metrics.currentValueContext: Active = phone is hot and performance is being reduced. Inactive = everything is normal.
metrics.healthyRange: Inactive is ideal. Brief throttling during heavy use is normal. Constant throttling suggests a problem.
metrics.commonCauses: High ambient temperature, sustained heavy load (gaming, video recording), blocked ventilation, case trapping heat.

metrics.label: Kernel Version
metrics.whatItMeasures: The version of the Linux kernel your Android OS is running on — the core bridge between software and hardware.
metrics.currentValueContext: This is the version string reported by the OS. Newer kernels have better security and hardware support.
metrics.healthyRange: Any officially supported version from your device manufacturer is normal.
metrics.commonCauses: Android OS updates, custom ROM installation, carrier-mandated kernel versions.

metrics.label: SELinux Status
metrics.whatItMeasures: Security-Enhanced Linux — Android's mandatory access control system. Enforced means security policies are active.
metrics.currentValueContext: Enforced = security policies active. Permissive = policies log but don't block (less secure).
metrics.healthyRange: Enforced is normal for production devices.
metrics.commonCauses: Custom ROMs may set permissive for compatibility. Some rooting methods disable SELinux enforcement.

metrics.label: Uptime
metrics.whatItMeasures: How long it's been since your phone was last restarted or powered on.
metrics.currentValueContext: Longer uptime means the phone hasn't had a fresh start recently. Good for stability, but occasional reboots help clear accumulated state.
metrics.healthyRange: Days to weeks is normal. Months without reboot may indicate OS updates are being skipped.
metrics.commonCauses: No recent restart, OS update pending, good stability, or significant uptime (user habit).

metrics.label: Kernel Wakelocks
metrics.whatItMeasures: System-level locks that prevent the phone from entering deep sleep. Each wakelock keeps some part of the hardware awake.
metrics.currentValueContext: Power Mode only. Each entry shows what's holding the phone awake and for how long. More wakelocks = more battery drain.
metrics.healthyRange: A few seconds per minute is normal. Multiple minutes of wake time means something is preventing sleep.
metrics.commonCauses: Apps with background services, push notifications, music playback, navigation, buggy apps not releasing wakelocks.

metrics.label: Hotspot Power Overhead
metrics.whatItMeasures: The additional power drain caused by using your phone as a WiFi hotspot or mobile tethering.
metrics.currentValueContext: Shown as estimated additional draw compared to normal usage without hotspot active.
metrics.healthyRange: Minimal when idle. Adds significant drain when actively passing data to connected devices.
metrics.commonCauses: Connected devices actively using internet, background sync on connected devices, poor cellular signal (hotspot uses more power to maintain connection).
